title: As-Sami' and al-Basir
hook: the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing, who hears whispers and sees the ant

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-'Alim, the All-Knowing, who knows what the heart hides. Your line was he already knows.

A woman in Medina has a bad problem at home. Her husband has said an old Arabian oath that leaves her neither married nor free. She comes to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and she argues. She pleads. She complains, out loud, to God. His wife Aisha is in the same room, and she said later that she could not even hear all of what the woman was saying. It was that quiet. Then verses came down that begin: God has heard the words of the woman who argued with you about her husband. The person in the room missed some of it. The one she was really talking to missed none of it.
screen: `A WOMAN ARGUES HER CASE.` → `AISHA CAN'T HEAR IT ALL.` → `GOD HAS HEARD.`

segments.voice: As-Sami': the All-Hearing, from sam', hearing. Al-Basir: the All-Seeing, from basar, sight. In the Qur'an they often come as a pair at the end of a verse, like two notes of one chord. One verse, in Pickthall's old translation: "Naught is as His likeness; and He is the Hearer, the Seer." First it says nothing is like him. Then it uses two words people use about themselves. Many Muslim scholars read it as a guard rail: God hears and sees, truly, but not with ears and eyes like ours. Human hearing gets tired; His doesn't. Human sight needs light; His doesn't. A saying often repeated in Muslim teaching has God seeing a black ant on a black stone on a moonless night. A picture, not a verse, but it makes the point: nothing is too small or too dark. And the pair isn't only about being watched. When Musa and Harun, Moses and Aaron, are sent to face Pharaoh, they're afraid, and God tells them not to fear: "Lo! I am with you twain, Hearing and Seeing." That's comfort, not surveillance. The woman in Medina had no lawyer, no power, no loud voice, and a complaint so quiet the person in the room missed some of it. The chapter she's remembered in is named for her: al-Mujadilah, the woman who argues. The Prophet taught that when people call on God, they're not calling someone deaf or far away. Heard. Seen. Even the whisper.
screen: `SAMI' — HEARING. BASIR — SEEING.` · `NOTHING IS LIKE HIM.` · `I AM WITH YOU, HEARING AND SEEING.` · `THE WOMAN WHO ARGUES.` · then, large: `HEARD. SEEN.`

segments.voice: Let the room go quiet and find the loudest sound, then a quieter one under it, then the quietest you can catch: a fridge, a breath, a bird far off. Open your eyes, find the smallest thing in view, a crumb, a thread, a speck of light, and hold the faintest sound and the smallest sight together. If you pray, you can call on God as as-Sami', al-Basir.
As-Sami', the All-Hearing: one of the two names, paired with al-Basir, the All-Seeing, that travel together through the Qur'an.
Your line: heard, seen. Even where no one seems to notice: a meeting, a group chat, a kitchen. Back tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims call on God as as-Sami' and al-Basir in private du'a, often quietly or silently, and many say after rising from bowing in prayer that God hears the one who praises him.

fork.setup: you're the woman in Medina. your husband's oath has left you stuck. nobody powerful is on your side. what do you do?
options: say nothing and put up with it.
bring your case to the Prophet and complain to God.
fork.reveal: she argued and complained to God, so quietly Aisha missed some of it, and a whole surah opens with God has heard her.

original.note: Arabic: the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing. from sam' (hearing) and basar (sight).

trapdoor: what you thought: God is watching you.
what it means: nothing is too quiet to be heard or too small to be seen, and the Qur'an mostly says it as comfort.
what a scholar hears: 42:11 sets the two names right after naught is as His likeness, so they're affirmed without picturing ears or eyes like ours.
recall: the one who grants safety and keeps faith
Peace itself: whole, safe, free from harm

sources.ref: Qur'an 58:1 (God has heard the woman who disputed with you about her husband)
Aisha's report that she could not hear all of Khawlah's words (Sunan Ibn Majah 188; Sunan an-Nasa'i 3460; cited by al-Bukhari in Kitab at-Tawhid)
hadith: you are not calling one who is deaf or absent (Sahih al-Bukhari 2992)

notes: Pickthall wording of 42:11 and 20:46 quoted from memory; please check against the 1930 text word for word.
The woman of 58:1 is usually named Khawlah bint Tha'labah and the oath as zihar; the script leaves both names out. Confirm the hadith references for Aisha's remark.
The 'black ant on a black stone on a moonless night' saying is presented as a saying, not a verse or sourced hadith; confirm that framing.
The guard-rail reading of 42:11 (affirming hearing and sight without likeness) is stated generally; different theological schools explain it differently. Confirm the neutral phrasing.
